title: Commissions of Inquiry — Nature, Powers and Limits

content.overview: Commissions of Inquiry under the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952 are fact-finding bodies appointed to inquire into matters of public importance. Their reports are recommendatory; they do not adjudicate rights or impose liability unless a separate statute so provides.
content.glance: Identify the commission and its terms of reference; state its fact-finding nature; note the recommendatory character of the report; distinguish from judicial or quasi-judicial adjudication.
content.study: A Commission of Inquiry is a statutory fact-finding body. It may summon witnesses and take evidence under the 1952 Act, but its conclusions do not bind courts or determine civil or criminal liability. Natural justice may apply to the extent the inquiry affects reputation, subject to the statutory framework and the nature of the proceedings. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952 and the specific notification appointing the commission.

sections.heading: Statutory Basis
sections.body: Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952 authorises appointment for matters of public importance.

sections.heading: Fact-Finding Character
sections.body: The commission investigates and reports; it does not adjudicate rights or impose sanctions.

sections.heading: Powers
sections.body: Powers to summon, examine and require production of documents as provided by the Act.

sections.heading: Report and Follow-Up
sections.body: The report is recommendatory; implementation depends on the appointing government and any subsequent legal process.

sections.heading: Fairness
sections.body: Procedural fairness may apply where reputation is engaged, within the statutory framework.

examples.title: Public-importance inquiry
examples.body: A commission is appointed to inquire into a major public incident. Its report may inform policy and further investigation but does not itself convict or award damages.

hypotheticals.question: Does a commission report create res judicata?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Findings are recommendatory and do not bind courts on liability issues.

hypotheticals.question: Can a person named in a report challenge it?
hypotheticals.analysis: Challenge may be available on jurisdictional, procedural or fairness grounds within established limits; the report itself is not a judicial decree.

distinctions.title: Commission of Inquiry vs court or tribunal
distinctions.right: Binding adjudication of rights or liability

misconceptions.trap: A commission of inquiry is a criminal court.
misconceptions.correction: It is a fact-finding body; it does not determine guilt or impose punishment.

misconceptions.trap: Commission findings are conclusive against named persons.
misconceptions.correction: Findings are recommendatory and do not create res judicata on liability.

cases.name: Tata Cellular v Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: Courts review legality of administrative processes.
cases.relevance: Judicial review remains available in respect of commission processes within established limits.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a commission-of-inquiry problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the commission and statute. II. State fact-finding nature. III. Note recommendatory character. IV. Address fairness if reputation is engaged. V. Conclude.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Statutory basis; terms of reference; nature of report; fairness/jurisdiction points; precise relief.
